summary: This neighborhood-stories piece surveys seven cultural landmarks created through immigration waves, each tied to a community: Italian, Chinese, Afro-Caribbean, Irish, Polish, Greek and Hispanic. For each it gives an opening or founding date, the people behind it, and the activities it hosts. The landmarks are presented as expressions of the neighborhood's multicultural identity.
one_line: A guide to seven immigrant-built cultural landmarks in the neighborhood, from Little Italy Piazza to the Hispanic Community Art Collective.
key_facts: The Little Italy Piazza arose from the Italian community that began settling in the area around September 7, 2023.
The Little Italy Piazza is anchored by a statue of philanthropist Giovanni Ferretti, unveiled on June 2, 2025.
The Chinatown Gateway Arch was inaugurated on January 18, 2024, with the Liu family instrumental in funding and designing it.
The Afro-Caribbean Cultural Center was founded on May 5, 2026, after Caribbean immigration waves in the early 2020s, spearheaded by community leader Marlon Baxter.
The Afro-Caribbean Cultural Center's grounds are the starting point of the annual Carnaval parade.
The Irish Memorial Garden was established on March 17, 2027, and features flora native to Ireland.
The Irish Memorial Garden's central piece is the sculpture "The Emigrant's Journey" by artist Siobhan Kelly.
The Polish Heritage Museum was established on October 10, 2025, a project propelled by Michalina Nowak.
The Polish Heritage Museum holds Polish folk costumes and wartime relics and hosts Pierogi-making workshops, film screenings, and guest lectures.
The Greek Amphitheater was opened on April 23, 2026, by Mayor Maria Kostas, a descendant of Greek immigrants.
The Hispanic Community Art Collective launched on September 15, 2023, during Hispanic Heritage Month.
The Hispanic Community Art Collective was founded by artists Diego Rivera and Lucia Fernandez and offers mural painting sessions and poetry slams.
